systeme:
Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}
contenu:
Format : long
Limite de longueur : 4500 caractères au total.
Édition numérique, lue sur téléphone, sans contrainte de page : la limite suit la matière disponible dans la source. Adapte le nombre de sections à la longueur : 2 sections sous 2 000 caractères, 3 ou 4 jusqu'à 3 500, 4 à 6 au-delà ; même règle de longueur (90 à 100 % de la limite). N'étire jamais une source mince : mieux vaut un article court et exact.
Source : Politico Europe
Rubrique : Europe
Date du flux : 09/11/2026
Auteur : Lennart Pfahler; Artur Weigandt
Titre d'origine : Disposable: The ordinary people doing Russia’s dirty work

ARTICLE :
The life Vasilij Kovacs knew ended with a bang. It was late afternoon on March 1, 2025, when an armored vehicle smashed through the metal gate of the old farmhouse where he lived southeast of the Latvian capital, Riga.
Masked men emerged with their guns drawn. They belonged to Latvia’s State Security Service, the country’s counterintelligence agency. The officers searched the property, seizing several mobile phones, SIM cards and documents, along with a pistol with its serial number filed off, a bayonet from an AK-47 and a cellphone jammer, according to a search report later filed by the authorities. They arrested Kovacs, a Ukrainian man in his 60s who has lived in Latvia for more than 30 years.
In March, Kovacs was transferred to stand trial in Lithuania, where he is accused of planning terrorist attacks, alongside four alleged accomplices. Five others face trial in Warsaw. Lithuanian and Polish prosecutors accuse the ten men of planning and carrying out arson attacks involving cargo parcels across several European countries on behalf of Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU.
One of those incidents made headlines across Germany. In the early hours of July 20, 2024, a parcel caught fire at Leipzig Airport just before it was due to be loaded onto a DHL cargo plane. The flames engulfed an airfreight container. It was probably only because the aircraft was delayed that the fire did not break out on board.
All ten men say they did not knowingly work for Russian intelligence and say they are innocent of the terrorism charges. According to investigative files from the Office of the Prosecutor General of Lithuania, Kovacs is an example of an increasingly common category of Russian intelligence asset — the kind Western intelligence agencies call “low-level agents,” or, more tellingly, disposable agents.
The 63-year-old Ukrainian national is alleged to have been a small cog in a much larger machine. Investigators say he transported massage pillows modified to be able to conceal incendiary devices from Latvia to Lithuania.
With its own officers finding it harder to operate in Europe since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the GRU increasingly relies on intermediaries to recruit people through messaging services such as Telegram, according to investigative files from Lithuania’s State Security Department obtained by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, of which POLITICO is a part of.
Often motivated by money, these disposable agents carry out individual assignments: Take a photograph. Mail a parcel. Move something from A to B. Sometimes the tasks are far more dangerous. Recruits may know little about the wider operation. Anyone who gets caught can be replaced.
Much has been written about these agents and the shadow war unfolding across Europe. But one perspective is usually missing: Who are these people? How did they become pawns in a new Cold War that is growing increasingly hot? Are they simply perpetrators — or are they victims, too?
For this article, we spoke to Kovacs several times, interviewed his daughter and examined thousands of pages of investigative records. Together, they reveal a sabotage network where meticulous intelligence planning goes hand in hand with human incompetence, and in which ordinary people are, well, disposable.
The GRU, contacted through the Russian government’s Press Service, did not reply to a request for comment.
The courier
The entrance to the prison where Kovacs has been held on remand for more than a year sits beneath a rusting metal roof. A Lithuanian investigating judge has authorized us to interview him, but when we arrive in September 2026, prison officers refuse to let us in. We need a separate document from the prison administration, they explain. We submit the additional paperwork but eventually have to leave.
A few days later, Kovacs calls from prison. He is allowed around 20 minutes on the phone each day, time he usually reserves for his family. But over the following weeks, he calls us repeatedly. “I also want to know how I ended up in here,” he says. He insists this is about justice, not himself. “I don’t value my own life particularly highly,” he says. “I’m not going to tell you how many times people have tried to kill me.”
There’s a lot about what Kovacs says during our conversations that’s unclear. But on one point, at least, his account and the investigators’ findings agree: He transported a package. Where they disagree is whether he knew what was inside it, what it was intended for — and who was behind the operation.
According to the Lithuanian investigative files, Kovacs’ involvement in the affair began on June 27, 2024, when someone contacted him on Telegram with a request.
He barely knew the man, but the two had been introduced by a mutual friend: Andrei Baburov, a former Russian submarine commander who was also the godfather of Kovacs’ 11-year-old son. The two men had met through their shared passion for the sea. Kovacs is a sailor who occasionally earns money delivering yachts for their owners. He says he first met Baburov while transporting a yacht between St. Petersburg and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
The request sounded harmless. A courier had fallen ill, and Kovacs was asked to collect a package and take it urgently to Vilnius, nearly four hours away by car. He agreed, collecting the package from a locker outside a supermarket in Riga using a code sent to him on Telegram by the man Baburov had introduced him to. He insists he was not paid. “If I’m helping someone I know, I do it for free,” he says.
That same day, he drove to Vilnius with his nephew. His contact on Telegram directed him to an underground parking garage. Kovacs parked outside, left the vehicle unlocked and walked away with his nephew. When they returned, the package had disappeared from the trunk. Kovacs says he had gone to buy a charging cable for his phone.
For Kovacs, that part of the job was done. But for the operation investigators have attributed to the GRU, things were only just getting started.
Burning parcels
Lithuanian investigators overseen by the Office of the Prosecutor General have reconstructed the movements of the devices used for the operation in painstaking detail, questioning witnesses and suspects, reviewing surveillance footage and digital evidence and analyzing DNA traces. The resulting files from the criminal investigation, compiling information from agencies in Lithuania, Latvia, Poland, Estonia, the U.K. and Germany, run at around 8,000 pages. They reveal a convoluted journey through the Baltic states, involving a succession of intermediaries, missed connections and improvised plans.
The man believed by Polish and Lithuanian investigators to have collected the package from Kovacs’ car was another Ukrainian, a trained chef who had spent five years in a Russian penal colony after being convicted of rape. By the summer of 2024, he was living in Poland and receiving instructions through Telegram from a handler who promised him €4,000 a month.
The following day, the chef allegedly took the massage pillows to a holiday apartment rented under a false name. He also had tubes of cosmetics filled with potentially explosive nitromethane. A video filmed inside the Airbnb apartment and later found on a suspect’s phone shows four boxes containing the massage devices and cosmetic products.
According to the Lithuanian investigative files, another intermediary was supposed to come and get the devices but could not find the entrance to the apartment complex. The chef’s handler changed the plan and ordered him to activate the ignition devices himself. The chef refused, according to an indictment filed by Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, obtained by the Global Reporters Network. The operation had to be reorganized.
Over the following days, the boxes passed through several more hands. At one point, Lithuanian investigators lost track of them altogether. They suspected they might have traveled through Moldova. On July 13, 2024, they resurfaced in Riga, where Kovacs was drawn into the operation for a second time.
Once again, according to his account, Kovacs received a Telegram call from the acquaintance he barely knew. This time, he said, he thought he could hear Baburov in the background. He was asked to transport another shipment to Lithuania, described as “high-quality massage pillows.” On July 17, he drove to Vilnius with his nephew.
There, another man collected his package and drove it to Kaunas, where on July 18 a Ukrainian who had traveled from Poland to Lithuania retrieved it. He, too, had a criminal past, having been convicted in Poland of cyber fraud and money laundering. His instructions came from a Telegram contact calling himself “Warrior.”
The Ukrainian packed four parcels containing the massage devices, tubes of potentially explosive cosmetics and various sex toys investigators believe were included as a distraction. He activated a timer and handed the parcels to the man who had previously failed to find the entrance to the holiday apartment. That afternoon, the man dropped off two parcels at a DHL office in Vilnius. They were addressed to Wimbledon in London and to Birmingham.
At 3:17 a.m. on July 20, customs officers in Leipzig inspected the parcel bound for London. They found nothing suspicious. The parcel was due to be loaded onto a plane to London. But at 5:45 a.m., it burst into flames while still on the ground. An expert report commissioned by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office, dated August 30, 2024, offered a terse assessment: “Fire caused by deliberate action: plausible.”
Two days later, the second parcel caught fire in a warehouse in Birmingham. That shipment, too, had previously been inspected by customs officers in Leipzig. They had found nothing.
The Ukrainian man also sent two other parcels to Poland through the DPD shipping service. In the early hours of July 21, one of them burst into flames inside a truck near Warsaw. Polish investigators recovered the other intact.
The Kremlin’s recruits
For investigators, the parcel operation is a case study in how Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, now organizes its operations in Europe. “The July 2024 incident fully corresponds to the modus operandi favored by the GRU in recent years when planning and conducting operations,” according to a report by Lithuania’s State Security Department, also known as the VSD, obtained by the Global Reporters Network.
For years, the GRU sent its own officers abroad to carry out covert operations. But that became increasingly difficult after the failed assassination attempt against former Russian double agent Sergei Skripal in Britain in 2018 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four years later. Now, the GRU leaves the dangerous work to others, increasingly relying on recruits directed through multiple layers of intermediaries.
At the top of the chain are still Russian intelligence officers. The Lithuanian report identifies Denis Smolyaninov, who, according to a decision to sanction him by the Council of the European Union, recruited operatives for sabotage missions in Europe through social media. The VSD considered it highly likely that Smolyaninov and two other GRU officers were involved in the parcel operation. Smolyaninov did not reply to a request for comment sent via the Russian Press Service.
The Lithuanian investigative files offered an unusually detailed picture of how the system worked. One of the alleged organizers was Andrei Baburov, the former submarine commander and godfather of Kovacs’ son. He allegedly coordinated the transport of the modified massage devices from Russia, drawing on old contacts, including former naval comrades and acquaintances in the Baltic states. Baburov did not reply to a request for comment.
Such personal connections are typical, according to the VSD. Recruits are often linked through “family or social ties,” the Lithuanian report says. Many have financial problems, no jobs or criminal records. They are recruited for individual assignments and do not necessarily know what lies behind them. The less they know, the less they can reveal if they are arrested. And anyone who gets caught can be replaced. “Their main motivation is the desire to make money quickly,” the report states.
Two years after the parcel attacks, operations of this kind had become a growing concern for European security agencies. In August 2026, two explosive-laden drones detonated at Leipzig/Halle Airport, while a third crashed into a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Among the suspects was a longtime acquaintance of Smolyaninov.
Shortly afterward, two Bulgarians allegedly threw incendiary devices near defense companies in Munich. Investigators suspected the GRU was behind the incident. In Romania, a fire broke out next to an arms factory. Starlink installations were set ablaze in Poland and Bulgaria, leading to further arrests. The GRU has seemingly turned the disposable-agent model into a mass-production operation.
Disposable
On the phone, Vasilij Kovacs sounds agitated. Speaking rapidly in Russian, he tries to explain himself, only to circle back over the same ground. “It was a crime committed so that it would be solved,” he says.
In Kovacs’ trial, the witnesses for the prosecution have already testified and the defense is preparing to call its own. With hearings scheduled well into January, a verdict is a long way off. Kovacs sees himself as the victim of a conspiracy. He believes the Russians deliberately drew him into the affair to make him, a Ukrainian citizen, a convenient villain. European investigators, he argues, only identified the most obvious participants without pursuing the people truly behind the operation.
He says it was Baburov who lured him into the trap, but he does not believe his former friend worked for the Kremlin. “They threw him away, too,” Kovacs said. Baburov, he says, was an opponent of the Russian government.
Kovacs is reluctant to answer questions about himself. Asked about his background, he says he was born in western Ukraine and had worked as a businessman. Had he worked at sea? “I’m just an amateur.” Then he interrupted: “But let’s move away from talking about me.”
He prefers to discuss what he sees as inconsistencies in the investigation. The weight of the massage pillows he transported does not match the weight of the parcels eventually shipped, he says. In his cell, he has filled a sheet of paper with tightly packed notes. Why are key figures behind the operation standing trial in Warsaw rather than Vilnius? What information was being withheld from the Lithuanian court? If the cargo had passed through Moldova, why was it not inspected at the border?
Other questions he’s less eager to address. What about the pistol with its serial number filed off, or the cellphone jammer found at his home? He was only renting the property, he says. They did not belong to him.
A photograph from the opening of his trial shows Kovacs sitting in the dock, unshaven, wearing a baseball cap beneath a hood. He looks tired. In another photograph, taken before his arrest, he sits on a motocross bike with his grandson perched in front of him, showing the boy how to hold the handlebars. He’s wearing the same cap, but with the bill turned backward. He looks carefree, almost boyish.
Viola Lisija, Kovacs’ 37-year-old daughter, knows the man in that photograph better than almost anyone. “He may be the person I’m closest to in my life,” she says. On the day he was arrested, she was supposed to meet him. She was at a playground in Riga with her son, now 7, when she learned what had happened. “My son loves his grandpa very much,” she says.
Her father had arrived in Latvia as the Soviet Union was collapsing. He initially worked in forestry before going into business, buying and selling forest land and acquiring stakes in Russian companies, including a shoe factory and an ice cream manufacturer. “Those were probably his best years,” Lisija said.
Around 2014, Russian authorities accused Kovacs of being a Ukrainian spy, according to his daughter. He was forced to stop traveling to Russia and give up his business interests there. Back in Latvia, he occasionally earned money sailing yachts from one port to another for their owners.
His background may help explain why Kovacs was of interest to the people behind the parcel operation. He had contacts in Russia, traveled between the Baltic countries and occasionally took on assignments. His daughter believed his previous troubles with the Russian authorities might also have made him a target.
Yet parts of her father’s life remained a mystery even to her. Had he ever moved in shady circles? “I really don’t know,” Lisija says. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, she noted, entrepreneurship and organized crime were often intertwined. Her father came from a different era. She says she never saw her father with a gun. “There were never any stories that made me think: Aha, he’s disappearing at night or doing something strange.”
Kovacs is struggling in prison. He has high blood pressure and complains of headaches. His family, too, is close to breaking point. Lisija’s son misses his grandfather. Every other day, the boy asks about him. She tells him Grandpa is at sea.
“I tell him he’s enjoying life to the fullest,” Lisija says. “I say, ‘He loves the sea, he’s a captain, and he’s off on long voyages around the world.’”
For now, at least, the boy believes her.
Lennart Pfahler is an investigative reporter at WELT. Artur Weigandt is a freelance journalist based in Prague.
The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, The Telegraph, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.
